originalTitle: Foldables are sort of boring now — and that’s great news for Apple

content: This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on smartphones and Android, follow Dominic Preston. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here. How it started Believe it or not, it didn’t all start with Samsung. Royole, a now-bankrupt manufacturer of flexible displays, was the first to release a commercial folding phone, the “charmingly awful” FlexPai. Samsung’s first Galaxy Fold followed a year later, plagued by a variety of faults that saw review units break within days. That launch went so badly that it prompted Chinese rival Huawei to delay the launch of its own Mate X foldable by five months; its unusual design with the foldable screen wrapped around the outside of the phone proved unpopular regardless. Motorola was next to join with its first Razr foldable, closely followed by Samsung’s similar Z Flip; we scored each 4/10 and 6/10 respectively. To say it was a rough first two years for foldable phones would be an understatement, but things did get better. Samsung’s subsequent generations of foldables didn’t break half as easily as the first wave, and it learned the valuable lesson that integral parts of the display stack shouldn’t be as easy to remove as a screen protector. More manufacturers joined the market, with foldables launched by Google, OnePlus, Oppo, Vivo, Xiaomi, Honor, and more. Prices slowly came down too — while flagship book-style foldables have hovered more or less around the $2,000 mark for seven years straight, cheaper models have appeared too. Motorola’s entry-level Razr is now $799, and last year Samsung introduced a cheaper FE variant of its Z Flip 7, for $899. The hardware evolved over that period too. Foldables got thinner, lighter, and more durable; the creases got flatter and less visible, while some displays began to include stylus support too; the cameras started to catch up to standard slab phones. Perhaps most importantly, the form factors began to shift too. How it’s going Until recently, foldable phones settled into two broad categories: compact flip phones, by now with square cover screens that extend across the outside of the phone’s front; and larger book-style foldables that are thin when shut and almost square when open.  This has slowly begun to change. Huawei was the first to push new designs, starting with its Mate XT trifold, then followed by a wider Pura X flip phone, and this year the Pura X Max, wider still. Samsung launched its own Galaxy Z TriFold late last year, and last month shifted its Galaxy Z Fold 8 to the same squat shape as the Pura X Max. Durability has improved to the point where Google’s Pixel 10 Pro Fold was able to introduce an IP68 rating; Honor’s Magic V6 has since one-upped that with IP69. That phone is also the thinnest foldable on the market, and the one with the largest battery, two feats that have been made possible by silicon-carbon battery designs, a more energy-dense technology that enables smaller batteries with larger capacities. The latest foldables are barely thicker than flagship slab phones when closed, and almost as thin as the USB-C port when open, while packing batteries that last a day or two per charge. Oppo’s Find N6 is almost as thin and long-lived as the Honor phone, but has another trick up its sleeve: an almost invisible crease. It’s still possible to see and feel the point where the inner screen folds, but only if you really hunt for it, and even then it can often be difficult to find depending on the light.  As for cameras, this remains the one area where foldables still have work to do, but not too much. Recent foldables from Oppo and Vivo have had triple rear cameras capable of impressive quality, comparable to some slab flagships. But they still lag behind the top tier of Ultra handsets, while costing substantially more. Still, this may be one area where foldables never fully catch up — cost and design constraints likely mean that the best of the best cameras will be limited to regular phones for the foreseeable future, with foldables always a step or two behind. Despite all these improvements, foldable phones remain an undeniably niche proposition: according to Counterpoint, they made up just 1.6 percent of the smartphone market in 2025. What happens next The tech behind foldable phones is now mature enough for even Apple to trust it: The first foldable iPhone is widely expected to debut next month alongside the iPhone 18 Pro models. The looming launch will be “a turning point for the foldable segment,” according to IDC analyst Francisco Jeronimo, in a report predicting Apple will claim 34 percent of the foldable market by value in its first year. What remains to be seen is whether Apple will have the influence to grow the foldable market, drawing in customers who were skeptical until now, or simply waiting for a foldable that runs iOS. This could be the tipping point that pulls foldables from a niche to the mainstream, though assuming Apple prices the phone at a premium, there will still be pretty strict limits to its reach. Even before its first sale, the foldable iPhone has already had an impact. Remember Huawei and Samsung’s wider folds? It’s probably no surprise that they appeared just months before Apple’s foldable, which leaks suggest will be similarly wide. More companies are likely to jump on the bandwagon, with leaks pointing to wider folds from both Oppo and Honor on the way. The next 12 months will be the test of whether this form factor is truly more popular with users, or if Android manufacturers will regret hopping on the Apple bandwagon. It’s less clear if more manufacturers will be making trifolds, or even whether Huawei and Samsung will stick with that form factor. Huawei has made bullish claims about the sales success of its two Mate XT phones, so there’s hope it will stick with the design. Samsung, on the other hand, pulled its TriFold from the market

chineseContent: 这是《The Stepback》，一份每周简讯，详细介绍了科技界的一个重要故事。有关智能手机和 Android 的更多信息，请关注 Dominic Preston。 《Stepback》将于美国东部时间周日上午 8 点到达我们订阅者的收件箱。在此处选择加入“后退”。不管你信不信，这一切并不是从三星开始的。柔宇科技（Royole）是一家现已破产的柔性显示器制造商，它是第一家发布商用折叠手机的公司，即“迷人而糟糕”的FlexPai。一年后，三星推出首款 Galaxy Fold，但由于受到各种故障的困扰，评测设备在几天内就出现故障。那次发布的情况非常糟糕，以至于促使中国竞争对手华为将自己的 Mate X 可折叠手机的发布推迟了五个月；事实证明，其不寻常的设计（将可折叠屏幕包裹在手机外部）并不受欢迎。摩托罗拉随后推出了首款 Razr 可折叠手机，紧随其后的是三星的类似 Z Flip；我们的得分分别为 4/10 和 6/10。说可折叠手机的前两年是艰难的，这还算轻描淡写，但情况确实有所好转。三星的后续几代可折叠设备并不像第一波产品那么容易损坏，并且它吸取了宝贵的教训，即显示屏堆栈的组成部分不应该像屏幕保护膜那样容易移除。更多制造商加入市场，谷歌、OnePlus、Oppo、Vivo、小米、荣耀等推出了可折叠手机。价格也慢慢下降——虽然旗舰书本式可折叠产品连续七年在 2000 美元左右徘徊，但更便宜的型号也出现了。摩托罗拉的入门级 Razr 现在售价 799 美元，去年三星推出了更便宜的 Z Flip 7 FE 版本，售价 899 美元。硬件也在那个时期不断发展。可折叠设备变得更薄、更轻
